source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Trend from the Open and Small Pullback Trends

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; 'session' means one trading day of intraday bars, boundary detected by Date(0) changing; standard Brooks setups referenced only by name in the chart walkthroughs (H1/H2/L1/L2, moving-average gap bar, wedge, double top/bottom, two-bar reversal, breakout pullback, final flag, 20 gap bar) are primitives from earlier chapters and are not redefined here

candidates.name: OpeningRangeHeightVsAverageDailyRange
candidates.quote: If the opening range of the day is less than 25 percent of the average daily range of recent days, there may be a double bottom on a bull trend day or a double top on a bear trend day.
candidates.description: Primitive with state: track the current session's opening-range high/low over its first N bars, and the average of the last M completed sessions' full-day range (high-low).
candidates.pseudocode: newSession = Date(0) != Date(1); if (newSession) { if (haveOpeningRange) pushDailyRange(sessionHigh - sessionLow); sessionHigh = high[0]; sessionLow = low[0]; barsIntoSession = 0; openingRangeSet = false } else { barsIntoSession++; sessionHigh = max(sessionHigh, high[0]); sessionLow = min(sessionLow, low[0]) } if (!openingRangeSet && barsIntoSession == openingRangeBars) { openingRangeHigh = sessionHigh; openingRangeLow = sessionLow; openingRangeHeight = openingRangeHigh - openingRangeLow; openingRangeSet = true } avgDailyRange = average(lastNDailyRanges, dayLookback)

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection and a rolling multi-day range history built from intraday bars, not a plain windowed average

notes: Same primitive as T22-01, redefined per this chapter's scope; the dedup pass should merge them.

candidates.name: QuarterOpeningRangePredictsDoubleBottomTrend
candidates.quote: The opening range was less than a third of the size of the range of recent days, and this put the market in breakout mode.
candidates.description: Filter: the opening-range height is below a small fraction of the recent average daily range (Brooks gives 25-33 percent), which favors a strong directional breakout that may begin with a double bottom (bull) or double top (bear) at the open rather than a gentle trending trading range.

complexity.reason: single comparison once T23-01's aggregates are available

notes: At ~50 percent instead, the book expects a trending trading range day (T22-02) rather than trend-from-open; verySmallFraction distinguishes the two.

candidates.name: TrendFromOpenFlag
candidates.quote: As soon as a bar moves above the high of the prior bar, the day is a trend from the open bull trend day, at least for that moment.
candidates.description: Primitive: a session flag, set long the first time a bar in the session closes above the high of the first bar (or of the prior bar early in the session), and cleared if price trades back through the session's opposite extreme. Cheap proxy for 'trend from the open' while it lasts.
candidates.pseudocode: newSession: trendFromOpen = 0; firstBarHigh/Low = high[0]/low[0] if (trendFromOpen == 0 && close[0] > firstBarHigh) trendFromOpen = 1; if (trendFromOpen == 0 && close[0] < firstBarLow) trendFromOpen = -1; if (trendFromOpen == 1 && close[0] < firstBarLow) trendFromOpen = 0 /* invalidated */

complexity.reason: per-session state machine anchored on the first bar

notes: Page 417: 'when the breakout of the prior bar grows into a larger spike, the odds of a strong trend from the open trend day increase considerably' - a stronger version could require an N-bar spike instead of a single close.

candidates.name: FirstPullbackAfterOpenSpikeEntry
candidates.quote: If the market trends from the first bar or so and the initial spike lasts three or more bars, entering on the first pullback is usually good for at least a scalp.
candidates.description: Entry: with the trend-from-open flag set and the opening spike at least N bars, buy on the first pullback that closes back above the pullback's signal-bar high (the first sideways or down move since the open).
candidates.pseudocode: trendFromOpen == 1 && spikeBarsSinceOpen >= minSpikeBars && isFirstPullbackSinceOpen && close[0] > high[1]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the pullback's signal bar

complexity.reason: reads the trend-from-open state plus a first-pullback-since-open counter

candidates.name: GapDirectionalBias
candidates.quote: When there is a large gap up and a trend from the open day forms, the day will be a bull trend day about 60 percent of the time and a bear trend day 40 percent of the time...The larger the gap, the more likely the day will be a trend day and the more likely the trend will be in the direction of the gap.
candidates.description: Soft filter: on a session that opens with a gap beyond a minimum size, prefer with-gap entries over against-gap entries (does not block the other side, just a bias weight/tie-break).
candidates.pseudocode: gapSize = open[0] - close[1]; abs(gapSize) >= minGapAtr * atr ? preferLongBias = (gapSize > 0) : preferLongBias = null
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context bias, not a hard gate)

complexity.reason: single gap-size comparison, but 'bias' rather than a gate is a design decision for the authoring pass

notes: The 60/40 split itself is a base rate, not a per-bar test; recorded as a directional tilt candidate, not a hard block.

candidates.name: PullbackSizeSinceTrendStart
candidates.quote: Look at the size of the pullbacks since the trend began. For example, in a small pullback bull trend, if the largest pullback in the past couple of hours has been only eight ticks, buy with a limit order at five to seven ticks below the high of the day.
candidates.description: Primitive with state: since the trend-from-open flag was set, track the largest pullback so far (the running high minus the lowest low reached before a new high, in a bull trend) as pullbackMax.
candidates.pseudocode: if (trendFromOpen == 1) { runningHigh = max(runningHigh, high[0]); if (high[0] < runningHigh) pullbackDepth = runningHigh - low[0]; pullbackMax = max(pullbackMax, pullbackDepth) }

complexity.reason: a running extreme and a depth-from-extreme tracker, reset each session

candidates.name: SmallPullbackTrendDayFlag
candidates.quote: This type of trend can be so strong that... the pullbacks in the Emini might be just 10 to 12 ticks (10 to 30 percent of the average daily range).
candidates.description: Filter: the day is a trend-from-open day and the largest pullback so far stays below a fraction of the average daily range -- the small pullback trend day variant, the strongest kind of trend day. Enables the weak-signal-bar allowance (T23-10) and the later-pullback expectation (T23-08).

complexity.reason: arithmetic once its component primitives are tracked

candidates.name: ExpectLargerPullbackAfterElevenAM
candidates.quote: About two-thirds of these days have a larger pullback after 11:00 a.m. PST. That pullback is often about twice the size of the biggest pullback since the trend began in the first hour.
candidates.description: Filter/context: on a confirmed small pullback trend day, once the session clock passes a cutoff time, a pullback of roughly 1.5-2x the day's largest prior pullback is expected and should not by itself be read as a trend reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: smallPullbackTrendDay && Time >= lateCutoffTime && currentPullbackDepth >= growthMultiple * pullbackMax

complexity.reason: a time gate plus the pullback-size ratio from T23-06/T23-07

candidates.name: FadeClimaxOnSmallPullbackDayAfterEleven
candidates.quote: If sometime between 11:00 a.m. PST and noon the market has two relatively large consecutive bull trend bars breaking out to a new high, the move is more likely an exhaustive buy climax than the start of a new leg.
candidates.description: Entry (countertrend, long side mirrored): after 11:00 a.m. on a small pullback bull trend day, two consecutive large bull trend bars break to a new high; short at (or a tick above) the close of the second one, expecting a two-legged, roughly 10-bar pullback.
candidates.pseudocode: smallPullbackTrendDay && Time >= lateCutoffTime && largeBullTrendBar[1] && largeBullTrendBar[0] && close[0] > highest(high, priorBars)[1]  /* long side is the mirror on a bear small-pullback day */
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at (or a tick beyond) the close of the second climax bar, scaling in higher

complexity.reason: combines the small-pullback-day regime filter with a two-bar climax pattern

notes: Similar in spirit to T21-38/T21-39/T22-07 (consecutive-climax fades); this variant is specific to the small pullback trend day regime and the 11am-to-noon window.

candidates.name: AllowWeakSignalBarsInConfirmedStrongTrend
candidates.quote: All pullbacks in trend from the open days are great with trend entries, even though they almost always look weak.
candidates.description: Research filter: when the small-pullback-trend-day flag is set, relax (or bypass) any normal signal-bar quality veto (small body, doji, countertrend body, heavy overlap) for with-trend entries, since Brooks says weak-looking signal bars are normal and reliable in this regime.

complexity.reason: requires the regime flag plus a design decision on which signal-quality checks it is allowed to override

candidates.name: TightenStopOnlyAfterNewExtremeFollowingPullback
candidates.quote: They should trail their protective stops below the most recent swing low only after the market pulls back to the area of the signal bar high and then rallies to a new high.
candidates.description: Exit-management rule: do not move a long's stop up to a new swing low's protection until price has both pulled back near the original signal bar's high AND then made a new trend high; moving the stop (or to breakeven) earlier gets the trade trapped out by normal-sized pullbacks in a tight channel.
candidates.pseudocode: if (!pulledBackToSignalBarArea) allowTighten = false; else if (high[0] > runningTrendHigh) { allowTighten = true; stopLevel = swingLow[1] }

complexity.reason: needs swing-low detection plus a two-part sequencing condition (retest then new extreme)

candidates.name: FixedStopPreferredInTightSmallPullbackChannel
candidates.quote: None of these pullbacks would have hit a two-point money stop, which is usually the best stop to use in a strong trend...it makes more sense to rely on the original two-point stop.
candidates.description: Exit: on a small pullback trend day, use a fixed price/ATR-based stop rather than a swing-low/prior-bar-low price-action stop, since the many small sideways bars get such stops hit too often.

complexity.reason: an ATR-scaled money stop, conditioned on the regime flag

candidates.name: FirstBarBreakoutEntry
candidates.quote: If there is a gap open that is more than just a few ticks and the first bar is a strong trend bar (small tail, good-sized bar), trading its breakout in either direction is usually a good trade.
candidates.description: Entry: the session's first bar is a strong trend bar (large body relative to range, small tails) following a gap; buy the breakout of its high at the next open.
candidates.pseudocode: barsIntoSession == 1 && abs(open[0] - close[1]) >= minGapAtr * atr && bullTrendBar[0]  /* enter next open on a stop above high[0] */
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the first bar's high

complexity.reason: session-relative bar index plus a gap size and trend-bar test

notes: Page 419: 'Even if there is not a gap open, a trend bar for the first bar is a good setup for a trade' - the gap requirement can be dropped (minGapAtr = 0) for that variant.

candidates.name: ReverseAfterFirstBarStopOut
candidates.quote: If you enter and your protective stop is hit on the next bar, consider reversing for a swing trade because the market will usually move more than the number of ticks that you lost on the first entry.
candidates.description: Entry: after the first-bar breakout trade (T23-13) is stopped out by the very next bar trading back through the first bar's opposite extreme, reverse into a position in the new direction.
candidates.pseudocode: firstBarBreakoutLongStopped == true /* the bar after entry closed below firstBarLow */ ? enterShortNextOpen : none

complexity.reason: reads the immediately-prior trade's outcome, which the engine already tracks via position state

candidates.name: FirstTrendLineBreakEntry
candidates.quote: The first pullback to break a trend line was bar 4. The first trend line break has a very good chance of being followed by another trend leg and is therefore a great entry.
candidates.description: Entry (short side, mirrored for a bull trend): in a confirmed trend from the open, the current bar's close breaks below the trend line drawn through the first two swing highs since the open for the first time this session; sell at the next open, expecting a second leg.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the break bar

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection, trend-line projection, and a 'first break this session' flag

notes: Page 409/440-ish: tiny pullbacks that don't break a meaningful trend line don't count as the 'first pullback' -- this is what makes it hard to identify in real time, per the book.

candidates.name: NoPauseByFourthBarIncreasesReversalOdds
candidates.quote: If the market does not pause by the third or fourth bar, it might have gone too far too fast, and this increases the chances that the market will reverse instead of trend.
candidates.description: Filter/context: if the first N bars of the session all extended in the same direction with no pause (no inside bar, no bar failing to make a new extreme), weight countertrend/reversal setups a bit higher for the next few bars instead of assuming trend continuation.
candidates.pseudocode: barsIntoSession >= noPauseBars && all of bars 1..noPauseBars made a new session extreme with no pause bar

complexity.reason: a short backward scan of session-relative bars against the pause-bar primitive

candidates.name: AvoidEntryAtScheduledReportTime
candidates.quote: Computers have a huge edge on reports...therefore should rarely enter at the moment a report is released.
candidates.description: Filter: block new entries within a short window of a known recurring report time (e.g. 7:00 a.m. PST economic data); wait for the bar containing the report to close and for the always-in direction to become clear.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(Time - reportTime) <= reportBlockMinutes -> block new entries this bar

complexity.reason: a Time comparison, but the report time is instrument/market-specific and not itself in OHLCV data -- treated as a fixed recurring parameter

notes: One-off events like an FOMC announcement do not recur at a fixed daily time and cannot be captured this way; only regularly scheduled data releases fit this pattern.

candidates.name: InitialLegMeasuredMoveReversalTarget
candidates.quote: Sometimes the market will make a measured move up equal to the open of the day to the low of the day and then close back down near the open...Other times the measured move up is equal to about the height of the entire initial leg down.
candidates.description: Exit: for a countertrend long taken after a trend-from-open sell-off reverses, take profit around a measured move projected from the reversal point, using the height of the initial leg down (open-to-low, or low-of-day-to-reversal-point) added to the reversal low.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the measured-move target

complexity.reason: arithmetic on remembered session levels (open, extreme, reversal point)

notes: Page 436 also gives a leg1 = leg2 variant: leg2 target = reversal point of leg1 + leg1's height, which is the general measured-move form used elsewhere in the corpus.

candidates.name: OppositeSpikeAtOpenBeforeRelease
candidates.quote: Once there was a spike down and a spike up after the first bar (a reversal down and then a reversal up), some traders would enter on a breakout, expecting the range to increase severalfold.
candidates.description: Primitive/filter: within the first few bars of the session, price spikes one way and then reverses and spikes the other way (an opening double top or double bottom) before the day's real trend is released; once this two-bar reversal high/low pair is in place, treat a break of either extreme as an entry with an increased-range expectation.
candidates.pseudocode: withinFirstBars(openingWindowBars) && openingSwingHighSet && openingSwingLowSet && (close[0] > openingSwingHigh || close[0] < openingSwingLow)
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the opening swing high / sell stop below the opening swing low

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection restricted to a short opening window

notes: Book prefers the more aggressive scalp-and-reverse variant (short the first spike, reverse long on the second, reverse short again on a failed breakout) over the textbook double-stop-order approach; both share this same opening double-extreme primitive.

rejected.quote: To an experienced trader, the swing setups are 70 percent or more likely to work...Most setups appear to have 50 percent or less probability of success.
rejected.reason: a discretionary, unverifiable success-rate claim about how setups 'look,' not a bar-level test

rejected.quote: Even the best patterns still fail to do what you expect about 40 percent of the time...Always be ready for the opposite of what might appear likely, because it will happen in about 40 percent of the time.
rejected.reason: a general base-rate observation, not a condition the engine can evaluate on a bar

rejected.quote: The chance of the first bar being the high or low of the day on a day when there is a large gap opening can be 50 percent or more...The high or low of the day forms within the first five bars or so in about 50 percent of days.
rejected.reason: background statistics about how often a pattern occurs, not itself an entry/exit condition

chapter_summary: Chapter 23 covers trend-from-the-open days and their strongest variant, the small pullback trend day, where pullbacks stay tiny all session and most signal bars look deceptively weak. The minable material is mostly regime detection built from a session-relative opening range and a running pullback-size tracker (T23-01/03/06/07), the entries and exits that regime licenses (first-pullback buy, first-bar breakout, first-trend-line-break, a late climax fade, measured-move targets), and management guidance (don't tighten stops too early, prefer fixed stops over price-action stops in a tight small-pullback channel, relax normal signal-bar quality checks once the regime is confirmed). Most of the chapter's chart walkthroughs (Figures 23.1-23.11) reuse named setups from earlier chapters (H1/H2/L1/L2, moving-average gap bar, wedge, double top/bottom, breakout pullback, two-bar reversal) and were not re-mined here; several base-rate percentage claims were rejected as non-mechanical.
